candidates.text:
New export of suspend function with JsExport

Previously, the @JsExport annotation did not allow exporting suspend functions (or classes and interfaces containing such functions) to JavaScript. You had to manually wrap each suspend function, which was cumbersome and prone to errors.

Starting with Kotlin 2.3.0, suspend functions can be exported directly to JavaScript using the @JsExport annotation.

Enabling suspend function exports reduces boilerplate and improves interoperability between Kotlin/JS and JavaScript/TypeScript (JS/TS). Kotlin's async functions can now be called directly from JS/TS without extra code.

sections: Use JavaScript code from Kotlin > Inline JavaScript

candidates.text:
Package structure

For most of the module systems (CommonJS, Plain, and UMD), Kotlin exposes its package structure to JavaScript. Unless you define your declarations in the root package, you have to use fully qualified names in JavaScript. For example:

package my.qualified.packagename

fun foo() = "Hello"

For example, when using UMD or CommonJS, your call site could look like this:

alert(require('myModule').my.qualified.packagename.foo())

When using plain as a module system setting, the call site would be:

alert(myModule.my.qualified.packagename.foo());

When targeting ECMAScript Modules (ESM), package information is not preserved to improve the application bundle size and match the typical layout of ESM packages. In this case, the consumption of the Kotlin declarations with ES modules looks like this:

import { foo } from 'myModule';

alert(foo());

candidates.text:
Isolating declarations in a separate JavaScript object in plain mode

If you have explicitly set your module kind to be plain , Kotlin creates an object that contains all Kotlin declarations from the current module. This is done to prevent spoiling the global object. This means that for a module myModule , all declarations are available to JavaScript via the myModule object. For example:

fun foo() = "Hello"

This function can be called from JavaScript like this:

alert(myModule.foo());

Calling the function directly like this is not applicable when you compile your Kotlin module to JavaScript modules like UMD (the default setting for both browser and nodejs targets), ESM , CommonJS , or AMD . In these cases, your declarations are exposed according to the chosen JavaScript module system. For example, when using UMD, ESM, or CommonJS, your call site would look like this:

alert(require('myModule').foo());

candidates.text:

Depending on the selected JavaScript Module system, the Kotlin/JS compiler generates different output. But in general, the Kotlin compiler generates normal JavaScript classes, functions, and properties, which you can freely use from JavaScript code. There are some subtle things you should remember, though.

candidates.text:
You must also annotate with @JsExport the corresponding actual implementation in the JavaScript source set, and it has to use only exportable types.

This fix allows shared code defined in commonMain to be correctly exported to JavaScript. You can now expose your multiplatform code to JavaScript consumers without having to use manual workarounds.

This change is enabled by default.

candidates.text:
Declare parameters with default values

If you are writing an external declaration for a JavaScript function which has a parameter with a default value, use definedExternally . This delegates the generation of the default values to the JavaScript function itself:

external fun myFunWithOptionalArgs(
    x: Int,
    y: String = definedExternally,
    z: String = definedExternally
)

With this external declaration, you can call myFunWithOptionalArgs with one required argument and two optional arguments, where the default values are calculated by the JavaScript implementation of myFunWithOptionalArgs .

result.answer:
Apply the `@JsExport` annotation to the top-level function to make it available from JavaScript [1]. The `@JsExport` annotation is currently the only way to make your functions visible from Kotlin [1]. You can use it together with the `@JsName` annotation to specify the names for the generated and exported functions, which helps resolve ambiguities in exports like overloads for functions with the same name [2].

Kotlin-only example:
```kotlin
@JsExport
fun greet(): String = "Hello"
```

Note that unless you define your declarations in the root package, the client must use fully qualified names in JavaScript for most module systems (CommonJS, Plain, and UMD) [4]. When targeting ECMAScript Modules (ESM), package information is not preserved, and consumption uses a plain named import like `import { greet } from 'myModule'` [4].

response.Answer:
{"status":"answered","answer":"Apply the `@JsExport` annotation to the top-level function to make it available from JavaScript [1]. The `@JsExport` annotation is currently the only way to make your functions visible from Kotlin [1]. You can use it together with the `@JsName` annotation to specify the names for the generated and exported functions, which helps resolve ambiguities in exports like overloads for functions with the same name [2].

Kotlin-only example:
```kotlin
@JsExport
fun greet(): String = "Hello"
```

Note that unless you define your declarations in the root package, the client must use fully qualified names in JavaScript for most module systems (CommonJS, Plain, and UMD) [4]. When targeting ECMAScript Modules (ESM), package information is not preserved, and consumption uses a plain named import like `import { greet } from 'myModule'` [4].","quotes":[{"chunk_id":"3e36da4b83ae9f33e669108aeee6a8671d7327481edcc5e401cf3f55d2ed1476","text":"By applying the @JsExport annotation to a top-level declaration (like a class, interface, or function), you can make Kotlin declarations available from JavaScript or TypeScript."},{"chunk_id":"3e36da4b83ae9f33e669108aeee6a8671d7327481edcc5e401cf3f55d2ed1476","text":"Currently, the @JsExport annotation is the only way to make your functions visible from Kotlin."},{"chunk_id":"f3b5957a3b87cac3b3102b6d12df9a4b744b31e0a9fb27b237066cfd984f174c","text":"Together with the @JsName annotation to specify the names for the generated and exported functions."},{"chunk_id":"3cd4266ae8db0369223e9c5dc5f409fdc2ae797f1a5d26c119b6c47a05530416","text":"Unless you define your declarations in the root package, you have to use fully qualified names in JavaScript."},{"chunk_id":"3cd4266ae8db0369223e9c5dc5f409fdc2ae797f1a5d26c119b6c47a05530416","text":"When targeting ECMAScript Modules (ESM), package information is not preserved to improve the application bundle size and match the typical layout of ESM packages."}],"clarification":""}

Kotlin types in JavaScript

See how Kotlin types are mapped to JavaScript ones:

Kotlin | JavaScript | Comments
Byte , Short , Int , Float , Double | Number | 
Char | Number | The number represents the character's code.
Long | BigInt | Set target = "es2020" or configure the -Xes-long-as-bigint compiler option .
Boolean | Boolean | 
String | String | 
Array | Array | 
ByteArray | Int8Array | 
ShortArray | Int16Array | 
IntArray | Int32Array | 
CharArray | UInt16Array | Carries the property $type$ == "CharArray" .
FloatArray | Float32Array | 
DoubleArray | Float64Array | 
LongArray | BigInt64Array | Set target = "es2020" or configure the -Xes-long-as-bigint compiler option .
BooleanArray | Int8Array | Carries the property $type$ == "BooleanArray" .
List , MutableList | KtList , KtMutableList | Exposes an Array via KtList.asJsReadonlyArrayView or KtMutableList.asJsArrayView .
Map , MutableMap | KtMap , KtMutableMap | Exposes an ES2015 Map via KtMap.asJsReadonlyMapView or KtMutableMap.asJsMapView .
Set , MutableSet | KtSet , KtMutableSet | Exposes an ES2015 Set via KtSet.asJsReadonlySetView or KtMutableSet.asJsSetView .
Unit | undefined | Exportable when used as return type, but not when used as parameter type.
Any | Object | 
Throwable | Error | 
enum class Type | Type | Enum entries are exposed as static class properties ( Type.ENTRY ).
Nullable Type? | Type , null , or undefined | 
All other Kotlin types, except for those marked with @JsExport | Not supported | Includes Kotlin's unsigned integer types .

candidates.text:
Use JavaScript code from Kotlin

Kotlin was first designed for easy interoperation with the Java platform: it sees Java classes as Kotlin classes, and Java sees Kotlin classes as Java classes.

However, JavaScript is a dynamically typed language, which means it does not check types at compile time. You can freely talk to JavaScript from Kotlin via dynamic types. If you want to use the full power of the Kotlin type system, you can create external declarations for JavaScript libraries which will be understood by the Kotlin compiler and the surrounding tooling.

candidates.text:
Additionally, it is important to know that:

Kotlin preserves overflow semantics for kotlin.Int , kotlin.Byte , kotlin.Short , kotlin.Char and kotlin.Long .

Kotlin cannot distinguish between numeric types at runtime (except for kotlin.Long ), so the following code works:

fun f() {
    val x: Int = 23
    val y: Any = x
    println(y as Float)
}

Kotlin preserves lazy object initialization in JavaScript.

candidates.text:
Usage of Long in exported declarations

Because Kotlin/JS used a custom Long representation, it was difficult to provide a straightforward way to interact with Kotlin's Long from JavaScript. As a result, you couldn't export Kotlin code that used the Long type to JavaScript. This issue affected any code using Long , such as function parameters, class properties, or constructors.

Now that Kotlin's Long type can be compiled to JavaScript's BigInt type, Kotlin/JS supports exporting Long values to JavaScript, simplifying the interoperability between Kotlin and JavaScript code.

Kotlin types in JavaScript

See how Kotlin types are mapped to JavaScript ones:

Kotlin | JavaScript | Comments
Byte , Short , Int , Float , Double | Number | 
Char | Number | The number represents the character's code.
Long | BigInt | Set target = "es2020" or configure the -Xes-long-as-bigint compiler option .
Boolean | Boolean | 
String | String | 
Array | Array | 
ByteArray | Int8Array | 
ShortArray | Int16Array | 
IntArray | Int32Array | 
CharArray | UInt16Array | Carries the property $type$ == "CharArray" .
FloatArray | Float32Array | 
DoubleArray | Float64Array | 
LongArray | BigInt64Array | Set target = "es2020" or configure the -Xes-long-as-bigint compiler option .
BooleanArray | Int8Array | Carries the property $type$ == "BooleanArray" .
List , MutableList | KtList , KtMutableList | Exposes an Array via KtList.asJsReadonlyArrayView or KtMutableList.asJsArrayView .
Map , MutableMap | KtMap , KtMutableMap | Exposes an ES2015 Map via KtMap.asJsReadonlyMapView or KtMutableMap.asJsMapView .
Set , MutableSet | KtSet , KtMutableSet | Exposes an ES2015 Set via KtSet.asJsReadonlySetView or KtMutableSet.asJsSetView .
Unit | undefined | Exportable when used as return type, but not when used as parameter type.
Any | Object | 
Throwable | Error | 
enum class Type | Type | Enum entries are exposed as static class properties ( Type.ENTRY ).
Nullable Type? | Type , null , or undefined | 
All other Kotlin types, except for those marked with @JsExport | Not supported | Includes Kotlin's unsigned integer types .

candidates.text:
Use JavaScript code from Kotlin

Kotlin was first designed for easy interoperation with the Java platform: it sees Java classes as Kotlin classes, and Java sees Kotlin classes as Java classes.

However, JavaScript is a dynamically typed language, which means it does not check types at compile time. You can freely talk to JavaScript from Kotlin via dynamic types. If you want to use the full power of the Kotlin type system, you can create external declarations for JavaScript libraries which will be understood by the Kotlin compiler and the surrounding tooling.

candidates.text:
Additionally, it is important to know that:

Kotlin preserves overflow semantics for kotlin.Int , kotlin.Byte , kotlin.Short , kotlin.Char and kotlin.Long .

Kotlin cannot distinguish between numeric types at runtime (except for kotlin.Long ), so the following code works:

fun f() {
    val x: Int = 23
    val y: Any = x
    println(y as Float)
}

Kotlin preserves lazy object initialization in JavaScript.

candidates.text:
You must also annotate with @JsExport the corresponding actual implementation in the JavaScript source set, and it has to use only exportable types.

This fix allows shared code defined in commonMain to be correctly exported to JavaScript. You can now expose your multiplatform code to JavaScript consumers without having to use manual workarounds.

This change is enabled by default.

Our goal is to design a Kotlin library consumed by browser JavaScript. Keep the target Kotlin/JS, not Wasm. By client I mean the browser JavaScript consumer. Use Kotlin-only code examples. How do I export a top-level function to the client?

Answer
Apply the `@JsExport` annotation to the top-level function to make it available from JavaScript [1]. The `@JsExport` annotation is currently the only way to make your functions visible from Kotlin [1]. You can use it together with the `@JsName` annotation to specify the names for the generated and exported functions, which helps resolve ambiguities in exports like overloads for functions with the same name [2].

Kotlin-only example:
```kotlin
@JsExport
fun greet(): String = "Hello"
```

Note that unless you define your declarations in the root package, the client must use fully qualified names in JavaScript for most module systems (CommonJS, Plain, and UMD) [4]. When targeting ECMAScript Modules (ESM), package information is not preserved, and consumption uses a plain named import like `import { greet } from 'myModule'` [4].

Use JavaScript code from Kotlin

Kotlin was first designed for easy interoperation with the Java platform: it sees Java classes as Kotlin classes, and Java sees Kotlin classes as Java classes.

However, JavaScript is a dynamically typed language, which means it does not check types at compile time. You can freely talk to JavaScript from Kotlin via dynamic types. If you want to use the full power of the Kotlin type system, you can create external declarations for JavaScript libraries which will be understood by the Kotlin compiler and the surrounding tooling.

result.answer: Yes. Applying the `@JsExport` annotation to a top-level declaration (like a class, interface, or function) makes Kotlin declarations available from JavaScript or TypeScript, and the annotation exports all nested declarations with the name given in Kotlin [1]. Regular Kotlin classes can be exported to JavaScript/TypeScript [3], and you can export a value class as a regular TypeScript class by marking it with `@JsExport` (together with `@JvmInline`) [2].

quotes.text: By applying the @JsExport annotation to a top-level declaration (like a class, interface, or function), you can make Kotlin declarations available from JavaScript or TypeScript. The annotation exports all nested declarations with the name given in Kotlin.
Previously, only regular Kotlin classes could be exported to JavaScript/TypeScript.

turns.answer:
Answer
Yes. Applying the `@JsExport` annotation to a top-level declaration (like a class, interface, or function) makes Kotlin declarations available from JavaScript or TypeScript, and the annotation exports all nested declarations with the name given in Kotlin [1]. Regular Kotlin classes can be exported to JavaScript/TypeScript [3], and you can export a value class as a regular TypeScript class by marking it with `@JsExport` (together with `@JvmInline`) [2].

Apply the `@JsExport` annotation to the top-level function to make it available from JavaScript [1]. The `@JsExport` annotation is currently the only way to make your functions visible from Kotlin [1]. Kotlin-only example:

```kotlin
@JsExport
fun greet(): String = "Hello"
```

Our goal is to design a Kotlin library consumed by browser JavaScript. Keep the target Kotlin/JS, not Wasm. By client I mean the browser JavaScript consumer. Use Kotlin-only code examples. How do I export a top-level function to the client?

Answer
Apply the `@JsExport` annotation to the top-level function to make it available from JavaScript [1]. The `@JsExport` annotation is currently the only way to make your functions visible from Kotlin [1]. You can use it together with the `@JsName` annotation to specify the names for the generated and exported functions, which helps resolve ambiguities in exports like overloads for functions with the same name [2].

Kotlin-only example:
```kotlin
@JsExport
fun greet(): String = "Hello"
```

Note that unless you define your declarations in the root package, the client must use fully qualified names in JavaScript for most module systems (CommonJS, Plain, and UMD) [4]. When targeting ECMAScript Modules (ESM), package information is not preserved, and consumption uses a plain named import like `import { greet } from 'myModule'` [4].

candidates.text:
Package structure

For most of the module systems (CommonJS, Plain, and UMD), Kotlin exposes its package structure to JavaScript. Unless you define your declarations in the root package, you have to use fully qualified names in JavaScript. For example:

package my.qualified.packagename

fun foo() = "Hello"

For example, when using UMD or CommonJS, your call site could look like this:

alert(require('myModule').my.qualified.packagename.foo())

When using plain as a module system setting, the call site would be:

alert(myModule.my.qualified.packagename.foo());

When targeting ECMAScript Modules (ESM), package information is not preserved to improve the application bundle size and match the typical layout of ESM packages. In this case, the consumption of the Kotlin declarations with ES modules looks like this:

import { foo } from 'myModule';

alert(foo());

candidates.text:
If we didn't specify the @JsName annotation, the name of the corresponding function would contain a suffix calculated from the function signature, for example hello_61zpoe$ .

Note that there are some cases in which the Kotlin compiler does not apply mangling:

external declarations are not mangled.

Any overridden functions in non- external classes inheriting from external classes are not mangled.

The parameter of @JsName is required to be a constant string literal which is a valid identifier. The compiler will report an error on any attempt to pass a non-identifier string to @JsName . The following example produces a compile-time error:

@JsName("new C()")   // error here
external fun newC()

candidates.text:
You must also annotate with @JsExport the corresponding actual implementation in the JavaScript source set, and it has to use only exportable types.

This fix allows shared code defined in commonMain to be correctly exported to JavaScript. You can now expose your multiplatform code to JavaScript consumers without having to use manual workarounds.

This change is enabled by default.

candidates.text:
Declare parameters with default values

If you are writing an external declaration for a JavaScript function which has a parameter with a default value, use definedExternally . This delegates the generation of the default values to the JavaScript function itself:

external fun myFunWithOptionalArgs(
    x: Int,
    y: String = definedExternally,
    z: String = definedExternally
)

With this external declaration, you can call myFunWithOptionalArgs with one required argument and two optional arguments, where the default values are calculated by the JavaScript implementation of myFunWithOptionalArgs .

candidates.text:
external modifier

To tell Kotlin that a certain declaration is written in pure JavaScript, you should mark it with the external modifier. When the compiler sees such a declaration, it assumes that the implementation for the corresponding class, function or property is provided externally (by the developer or via an npm dependency ), and therefore does not try to generate any JavaScript code from the declaration. This is also why external declarations can't have a body. For example:

external fun alert(message: Any?): Unit

external class Node {
    val firstChild: Node

    fun append(child: Node): Node

    fun removeChild(child: Node): Node

    // etc
}

external val window: Window

Note that the external modifier is inherited by nested declarations. This is why in the example Node class, there is no external modifier before member functions and properties.

The external modifier is only allowed on package-level declarations. You can't declare an external member of a non- external class.

candidates.text:
Isolating declarations in a separate JavaScript object in plain mode

If you have explicitly set your module kind to be plain , Kotlin creates an object that contains all Kotlin declarations from the current module. This is done to prevent spoiling the global object. This means that for a module myModule , all declarations are available to JavaScript via the myModule object. For example:

fun foo() = "Hello"

This function can be called from JavaScript like this:

alert(myModule.foo());

Calling the function directly like this is not applicable when you compile your Kotlin module to JavaScript modules like UMD (the default setting for both browser and nodejs targets), ESM , CommonJS , or AMD . In these cases, your declarations are exposed according to the chosen JavaScript module system. For example, when using UMD, ESM, or CommonJS, your call site would look like this:

alert(require('myModule').foo());

Function names

Names of functions, properties, and local variables start with a lowercase letter and use camel case without underscores:

fun processDeclarations() { /*...*/ }

candidates.text:
Property names

Names of constants (properties marked with const , or top-level or object val properties with no custom get function that hold deeply immutable data) should use all uppercase, underscore-separated names following the screaming snake case convention:

const val MAX_COUNT = 8
val USER_NAME_FIELD = "UserName"

Names of top-level or object properties which hold objects with behavior or mutable data should use camel case names:

val mutableCollection: MutableSet<String> = HashSet()

Names of properties holding references to singleton objects can use the same naming style as object declarations:

val PersonComparator: Comparator<Person> = /*...*/

candidates.text:
Deprecation of default exports

As part of the migration to named exports, an error was previously printed to the console when a default import was used for Kotlin/Wasm exports in JavaScript.

In 2.1.0, default imports have been completely removed to fully support named exports.

When coding in JavaScript for the Kotlin/Wasm target, you now need to use the corresponding named imports instead of default imports.

This change marks the last phase of a deprecation cycle to migrate to named exports:

In version 2.0.0: A warning message was printed to the console, explaining that exporting entities via default exports is deprecated.

In version 2.0.20: An error occurred, requesting the use of the corresponding named import.

In version 2.1.0: The use of default imports has been completely removed.

candidates.text:
Package structure

For most of the module systems (CommonJS, Plain, and UMD), Kotlin exposes its package structure to JavaScript. Unless you define your declarations in the root package, you have to use fully qualified names in JavaScript. For example:

package my.qualified.packagename

fun foo() = "Hello"

For example, when using UMD or CommonJS, your call site could look like this:

alert(require('myModule').my.qualified.packagename.foo())

When using plain as a module system setting, the call site would be:

alert(myModule.my.qualified.packagename.foo());

When targeting ECMAScript Modules (ESM), package information is not preserved to improve the application bundle size and match the typical layout of ESM packages. In this case, the consumption of the Kotlin declarations with ES modules looks like this:

import { foo } from 'myModule';

alert(foo());

candidates.text:
If we didn't specify the @JsName annotation, the name of the corresponding function would contain a suffix calculated from the function signature, for example hello_61zpoe$ .

Note that there are some cases in which the Kotlin compiler does not apply mangling:

external declarations are not mangled.

Any overridden functions in non- external classes inheriting from external classes are not mangled.

The parameter of @JsName is required to be a constant string literal which is a valid identifier. The compiler will report an error on any attempt to pass a non-identifier string to @JsName . The following example produces a compile-time error:

@JsName("new C()")   // error here
external fun newC()

This fix allows shared code defined in commonMain to be correctly exported to JavaScript. You can now expose your multiplatform code to JavaScript consumers without having to use manual workarounds.

This change is enabled by default.

candidates.text:
Declare parameters with default values

If you are writing an external declaration for a JavaScript function which has a parameter with a default value, use definedExternally . This delegates the generation of the default values to the JavaScript function itself:

external fun myFunWithOptionalArgs(
    x: Int,
    y: String = definedExternally,
    z: String = definedExternally
)

With this external declaration, you can call myFunWithOptionalArgs with one required argument and two optional arguments, where the default values are calculated by the JavaScript implementation of myFunWithOptionalArgs .

candidates.text:
external modifier

To tell Kotlin that a certain declaration is written in pure JavaScript, you should mark it with the external modifier. When the compiler sees such a declaration, it assumes that the implementation for the corresponding class, function or property is provided externally (by the developer or via an npm dependency ), and therefore does not try to generate any JavaScript code from the declaration. This is also why external declarations can't have a body. For example:

external fun alert(message: Any?): Unit

external class Node {
    val firstChild: Node

    fun append(child: Node): Node

    fun removeChild(child: Node): Node

    // etc
}

external val window: Window

Note that the external modifier is inherited by nested declarations. This is why in the example Node class, there is no external modifier before member functions and properties.

The external modifier is only allowed on package-level declarations. You can't declare an external member of a non- external class.

candidates.text:
Isolating declarations in a separate JavaScript object in plain mode

If you have explicitly set your module kind to be plain , Kotlin creates an object that contains all Kotlin declarations from the current module. This is done to prevent spoiling the global object. This means that for a module myModule , all declarations are available to JavaScript via the myModule object. For example:

fun foo() = "Hello"

This function can be called from JavaScript like this:

alert(myModule.foo());

Calling the function directly like this is not applicable when you compile your Kotlin module to JavaScript modules like UMD (the default setting for both browser and nodejs targets), ESM , CommonJS , or AMD . In these cases, your declarations are exposed according to the chosen JavaScript module system. For example, when using UMD, ESM, or CommonJS, your call site would look like this:

alert(require('myModule').foo());

turns.answer:
Answer
Use the `@JsName` annotation to control the generated JavaScript name for an exported declaration [2]. The Kotlin compiler otherwise mangles the names of generated functions and attributes in JavaScript code — for example, without `@JsName` the corresponding function name would contain a suffix calculated from the function signature, such as `hello_61zpoe$` [2][4]. `@JsName` likewise lets you specify the names for the generated and exported functions, which helps resolve ambiguities in exports like overloads for functions with the same name [1].

The parameter of `@JsName` is required to be a constant string literal which is a valid identifier; the compiler reports an error for a non-identifier string [4].

Kotlin-only example:
```kotlin
class Person(val name: String) {
    fun hello() {
        println("Hello $name!")
    }

    @JsName("helloWithGreeting")
    fun hello(greeting: String) {
        println("$greeting $name!")
    }
}
```
This example is taken verbatim from the documentation, where the client uses `person.hello()` and `person.helloWithGreeting("Servus")` [2].

If your goal is a default export specifically, a separate annotation `@JsExport.Default` applied to a Kotlin declaration (class, object, function, or property) makes the generated JavaScript automatically include an `export default` statement for ES modules; for module systems different from ES modules, `@JsExport.Default` works similarly to the regular `@JsExport` annotation [3].

Our goal is to design a Kotlin library consumed by browser JavaScript. Keep the target Kotlin/JS, not Wasm. By client I mean the browser JavaScript consumer. Use Kotlin-only code examples. How do I export a top-level function to the client?

Answer
Apply the `@JsExport` annotation to the top-level function to make it available from JavaScript [1]. The `@JsExport` annotation is currently the only way to make your functions visible from Kotlin [1]. You can use it together with the `@JsName` annotation to specify the names for the generated and exported functions, which helps resolve ambiguities in exports like overloads for functions with the same name [2].

Kotlin-only example:
```kotlin
@JsExport
fun greet(): String = "Hello"
```

Note that unless you define your declarations in the root package, the client must use fully qualified names in JavaScript for most module systems (CommonJS, Plain, and UMD) [4]. When targeting ECMAScript Modules (ESM), package information is not preserved, and consumption uses a plain named import like `import { greet } from 'myModule'` [4].

Can I export a class for the client in the same way?

Answer
Yes. Applying the `@JsExport` annotation to a top-level declaration (like a class, interface, or function) makes Kotlin declarations available from JavaScript or TypeScript, and the annotation exports all nested declarations with the name given in Kotlin [1]. Regular Kotlin classes can be exported to JavaScript/TypeScript [3], and you can export a value class as a regular TypeScript class by marking it with `@JsExport` (together with `@JvmInline`) [2].

@JsName annotation

In some cases (for example, to support overloads), the Kotlin compiler mangles the names of generated functions and attributes in JavaScript code. To control the generated names, you can use the @JsName annotation:

// Module 'kjs'
class Person(val name: String) {
    fun hello() {
        println("Hello $name!")
    }

    @JsName("helloWithGreeting")
    fun hello(greeting: String) {
        println("$greeting $name!")
    }
}

Now you can use this class from JavaScript in the following way:

// If necessary, import 'kjs' according to chosen module system
var person = new kjs.Person("Dmitry");   // refers to module 'kjs'
person.hello();                          // prints "Hello Dmitry!"
person.helloWithGreeting("Servus");      // prints "Servus Dmitry!"

[3] What's new in Kotlin 2.3.0 — What's new in Kotlin 2.3.0 > Kotlin/JS > Support for JavaScript default exports
https://kotlinlang.org/docs/whatsnew23.html (normalized source lines 540-560; release 2.3.0; availability See individual feature status in source; release version is not a snippet compatibility guarantee.; chunk_id: d7cc1096c9a709fbd88dc299c92a26d0462a72c986688d42c6f608c97081a277)
Support for JavaScript default exports

Previously, Kotlin/JS could not generate JavaScript's default exports from Kotlin code. Instead, Kotlin/JS only generated named exports, for example:

export { SomeDeclaration };

If you required a default export, you had to use workarounds inside the compiler, such as placing the @JsName annotation with default and a space as an argument:

@JsExport
@JsName("default ")
class SomeDeclaration

Kotlin/JS now supports default exports directly through a new annotation:

@JsExport.Default

When you apply this annotation to a Kotlin declaration (class, object, function, or property), the generated JavaScript automatically includes an export default statement for ES modules:

export default HelloWorker;

For module systems different from ES modules, the new @JsExport.Default annotation works similarly to the regular @JsExport annotation.

[4] Use Kotlin code from JavaScript — Use Kotlin code from JavaScript > Package structure > @JsName annotation
https://kotlinlang.org/docs/js-to-kotlin-interop.html (normalized source lines 66-77; release unknown; availability unknown; chunk_id: c4865e5aee3668f6f35e5d43cb0df8200d3cf39c04d21e8656f080fccb831cf5)
If we didn't specify the @JsName annotation, the name of the corresponding function would contain a suffix calculated from the function signature, for example hello_61zpoe$ .

Note that there are some cases in which the Kotlin compiler does not apply mangling:

external declarations are not mangled.

Any overridden functions in non- external classes inheriting from external classes are not mangled.

The parameter of @JsName is required to be a constant string literal which is a valid identifier. The compiler will report an error on any attempt to pass a non-identifier string to @JsName . The following example produces a compile-time error:

@JsName("new C()")   // error here
external fun newC()

You must also annotate with @JsExport the corresponding actual implementation in the JavaScript source set, and it has to use only exportable types.

This fix allows shared code defined in commonMain to be correctly exported to JavaScript. You can now expose your multiplatform code to JavaScript consumers without having to use manual workarounds.

This change is enabled by default.

candidates.text:
Use JavaScript code from Kotlin

Kotlin was first designed for easy interoperation with the Java platform: it sees Java classes as Kotlin classes, and Java sees Kotlin classes as Java classes.

However, JavaScript is a dynamically typed language, which means it does not check types at compile time. You can freely talk to JavaScript from Kotlin via dynamic types. If you want to use the full power of the Kotlin type system, you can create external declarations for JavaScript libraries which will be understood by the Kotlin compiler and the surrounding tooling.

See how Kotlin types are mapped to JavaScript ones:

Kotlin | JavaScript | Comments
Byte , Short , Int , Float , Double | Number | 
Char | Number | The number represents the character's code.
Long | BigInt | Set target = "es2020" or configure the -Xes-long-as-bigint compiler option .
Boolean | Boolean | 
String | String | 
Array | Array | 
ByteArray | Int8Array | 
ShortArray | Int16Array | 
IntArray | Int32Array | 
CharArray | UInt16Array | Carries the property $type$ == "CharArray" .
FloatArray | Float32Array | 
DoubleArray | Float64Array | 
LongArray | BigInt64Array | Set target = "es2020" or configure the -Xes-long-as-bigint compiler option .
BooleanArray | Int8Array | Carries the property $type$ == "BooleanArray" .
List , MutableList | KtList , KtMutableList | Exposes an Array via KtList.asJsReadonlyArrayView or KtMutableList.asJsArrayView .
Map , MutableMap | KtMap , KtMutableMap | Exposes an ES2015 Map via KtMap.asJsReadonlyMapView or KtMutableMap.asJsMapView .
Set , MutableSet | KtSet , KtMutableSet | Exposes an ES2015 Set via KtSet.asJsReadonlySetView or KtMutableSet.asJsSetView .
Unit | undefined | Exportable when used as return type, but not when used as parameter type.
Any | Object |

candidates.text:
New export of suspend function with JsExport

Previously, the @JsExport annotation did not allow exporting suspend functions (or classes and interfaces containing such functions) to JavaScript. You had to manually wrap each suspend function, which was cumbersome and prone to errors.

Starting with Kotlin 2.3.0, suspend functions can be exported directly to JavaScript using the @JsExport annotation.

Enabling suspend function exports reduces boilerplate and improves interoperability between Kotlin/JS and JavaScript/TypeScript (JS/TS). Kotlin's async functions can now be called directly from JS/TS without extra code.

But in general, the Kotlin compiler generates normal JavaScript classes, functions, and properties, which you can freely use from JavaScript code. There are some subtle things you should remember, though.

How do I export a top-level function to the client?"},{"role":"assistant","content":"Answer
Apply the `@JsExport` annotation to the top-level function to make it available from JavaScript [1]. The `@JsExport` annotation is currently the only way to make your functions visible from Kotlin [1]. You can use it together with the `@JsName` annotation to specify the names for the generated and exported functions, which helps resolve ambiguities in exports like overloads for functions with the same name [2].

Kotlin-only example:
```kotlin
@JsExport
fun greet(): String = "Hello"
```

Note that unless you define your declarations in the root package, the client must use fully qualified names in JavaScript for most module systems (CommonJS, Plain, and UMD) [4]. When targeting ECMAScript Modules (ESM), package information is not preserved, and consumption uses a plain named import like `import { greet } from 'myModule'` [4].

> To export a value class, mark it with the @JsExport annotation on the Kotlin side:"},{"role":"user","content":"How should I give an exported declaration a predictable JavaScript name?"},{"role":"assistant","content":"Answer
Use the `@JsName` annotation to control the generated JavaScript name for an exported declaration [2]. The Kotlin compiler otherwise mangles the names of generated functions and attributes in JavaScript code — for example, without `@JsName` the corresponding function name would contain a suffix calculated from the function signature, such as `hello_61zpoe$` [2][4]. `@JsName` likewise lets you specify the names for the generated and exported functions, which helps resolve ambiguities in exports like overloads for functions with the same name [1].

The parameter of `@JsName` is required to be a constant string literal which is a valid identifier; the compiler reports an error for a non-identifier string [4].

Kotlin-only example:
```kotlin
class Person(val name: String) {
    fun hello() {
        println("Hello $name!")
    }

    @JsName("helloWithGreeting")
    fun hello(greeting: String) {
        println("$greeting $name!")
    }
}
```
This example is taken verbatim from the documentation, where the client uses `person.hello()` and `person.helloWithGreeting("Servus")` [2].

If your goal is a default export specifically, a separate annotation `@JsExport.Default` applied to a Kotlin declaration (class, object, function, or property) makes the generated JavaScript automatically include an `export default` statement for ES modules; for module systems different from ES modules, `@JsExport.Default` works similarly to the regular `@JsExport` annotation [3].

You can export Kotlin interfaces to JavaScript/TypeScript with the @JsNoRuntime annotation. It allows for direct mapping to regular TypeScript interfaces.

To export a Kotlin interface, for example, from a Kotlin Multiplatform project:

Annotate the Kotlin interface with @JsNoRuntime in common code:

// commonMain
import kotlin.js.JsNoRuntime

@JsNoRuntime
expect interface DataProcessor {
    fun process(data: String): Int 
}

Provide the actual implementation with @JsNoRuntime in your JS-specific source code:

// jsMain
import kotlin.js.JsNoRuntime

@JsNoRuntime
actual interface DataProcessor {
    actual fun process(data: String): Int
} ","title":"Use Kotlin code from JavaScript","source":"https://kotlinlang.org/docs/js-to-kotlin-interop.html","sections":["Use Kotlin code from JavaScript > Package structure > @JsNoRuntime annotation"],"line_start":170,"line_end":194,"score":0.5266708135604858,"release_version":null,"availability":"unknown"},{"anchor":"new-export-of-suspend-function-with-jsexport","start":17332,"end":17954,"split_code":false,"platforms":["common","jvm","android","native","js","wasm"],"id":"72aac8f3d4897743b042472b067c4ba3f44643ff24a22122085cd8a0c18ec2c0","document_id":"whatsnew23","strategy":"semantic","text":"New export of suspend function with JsExport

Starting with Kotlin 2.3.0, suspend functions can be exported directly to JavaScript using the @JsExport annotation.

Previously, when you tried to export a function returning the Promise<Unit> type with the @JsExport annotation, the Kotlin compiler produced an error.

While return types like Promise<Int> worked correctly, using Promise<Unit> triggered a "non-exportable type" warning, even though it correctly mapped to Promise<void> in TypeScript.

This restriction has been removed. Now, the following code compiles without error:

// Worked correctly before
@JsExport
fun fooInt(): Promise<Int> = GlobalScope.promise {
    delay(100)
    return@promise 42
}

// Produced error, but now works correctly
@JsExport
fun fooUnit(): Promise<Unit> = GlobalScope.promise {
    delay(100)

Our goal is to design a Kotlin library consumed by browser JavaScript. Keep the target Kotlin/JS, not Wasm. By client I mean the browser JavaScript consumer. Use Kotlin-only code examples. How do I export a top-level function to the client?

Answer
Apply the `@JsExport` annotation to the top-level function to make it available from JavaScript [1]. The `@JsExport` annotation is currently the only way to make your functions visible from Kotlin [1]. You can use it together with the `@JsName` annotation to specify the names for the generated and exported functions, which helps resolve ambiguities in exports like overloads for functions with the same name [2].

Kotlin-only example:
```kotlin
@JsExport
fun greet(): String = "Hello"
```

Note that unless you define your declarations in the root package, the client must use fully qualified names in JavaScript for most module systems (CommonJS, Plain, and UMD) [4]. When targeting ECMAScript Modules (ESM), package information is not preserved, and consumption uses a plain named import like `import { greet } from 'myModule'` [4].

Can I export a class for the client in the same way?

Answer
Yes. Applying the `@JsExport` annotation to a top-level declaration (like a class, interface, or function) makes Kotlin declarations available from JavaScript or TypeScript, and the annotation exports all nested declarations with the name given in Kotlin [1]. Regular Kotlin classes can be exported to JavaScript/TypeScript [3], and you can export a value class as a regular TypeScript class by marking it with `@JsExport` (together with `@JvmInline`) [2].

How should I give an exported declaration a predictable JavaScript name?

Answer
Use the `@JsName` annotation to control the generated JavaScript name for an exported declaration [2]. The Kotlin compiler otherwise mangles the names of generated functions and attributes in JavaScript code — for example, without `@JsName` the corresponding function name would contain a suffix calculated from the function signature, such as `hello_61zpoe$` [2][4]. `@JsName` likewise lets you specify the names for the generated and exported functions, which helps resolve ambiguities in exports like overloads for functions with the same name [1].

The parameter of `@JsName` is required to be a constant string literal which is a valid identifier; the compiler reports an error for a non-identifier string [4].

Kotlin-only example:
```kotlin
class Person(val name: String) {
    fun hello() {
        println("Hello $name!")
    }

    @JsName("helloWithGreeting")
    fun hello(greeting: String) {
        println("$greeting $name!")
    }
}
```
This example is taken verbatim from the documentation, where the client uses `person.hello()` and `person.helloWithGreeting("Servus")` [2].

If your goal is a default export specifically, a separate annotation `@JsExport.Default` applied to a Kotlin declaration (class, object, function, or property) makes the generated JavaScript automatically include an `export default` statement for ES modules; for module systems different from ES modules, `@JsExport.Default` works similarly to the regular `@JsExport` annotation [3].

candidates.text:
Use JavaScript code from Kotlin

Kotlin was first designed for easy interoperation with the Java platform: it sees Java classes as Kotlin classes, and Java sees Kotlin classes as Java classes.

However, JavaScript is a dynamically typed language, which means it does not check types at compile time. You can freely talk to JavaScript from Kotlin via dynamic types. If you want to use the full power of the Kotlin type system, you can create external declarations for JavaScript libraries which will be understood by the Kotlin compiler and the surrounding tooling.
candidates.title: Use JavaScript code from Kotlin
sections: Use JavaScript code from Kotlin

candidates.text:
Isolating declarations in a separate JavaScript object in plain mode

If you have explicitly set your module kind to be plain , Kotlin creates an object that contains all Kotlin declarations from the current module. This is done to prevent spoiling the global object. This means that for a module myModule , all declarations are available to JavaScript via the myModule object. For example:

fun foo() = "Hello"

This function can be called from JavaScript like this:

alert(myModule.foo());

Calling the function directly like this is not applicable when you compile your Kotlin module to JavaScript modules like UMD (the default setting for both browser and nodejs targets), ESM , CommonJS , or AMD . In these cases, your declarations are exposed according to the chosen JavaScript module system. For example, when using UMD, ESM, or CommonJS, your call site would look like this:

alert(require('myModule').foo());
candidates.title: Use Kotlin code from JavaScript
sections: Use Kotlin code from JavaScript > Isolating declarations in a separate JavaScript object in plain mode

candidates.text:
Package structure

For most of the module systems (CommonJS, Plain, and UMD), Kotlin exposes its package structure to JavaScript. Unless you define your declarations in the root package, you have to use fully qualified names in JavaScript. For example:

package my.qualified.packagename

fun foo() = "Hello"

For example, when using UMD or CommonJS, your call site could look like this:

alert(require('myModule').my.qualified.packagename.foo())

When using plain as a module system setting, the call site would be:

alert(myModule.my.qualified.packagename.foo());

When targeting ECMAScript Modules (ESM), package information is not preserved to improve the application bundle size and match the typical layout of ESM packages. In this case, the consumption of the Kotlin declarations with ES modules looks like this:

import { foo } from 'myModule';

alert(foo());

candidates.text:
Declare parameters with default values

If you are writing an external declaration for a JavaScript function which has a parameter with a default value, use definedExternally . This delegates the generation of the default values to the JavaScript function itself:

external fun myFunWithOptionalArgs(
    x: Int,
    y: String = definedExternally,
    z: String = definedExternally
)

With this external declaration, you can call myFunWithOptionalArgs with one required argument and two optional arguments, where the default values are calculated by the JavaScript implementation of myFunWithOptionalArgs .

Deprecate legacy Kotlin/JS compiler type selection APIs

Issue : KT-64275 , KT-84753

Component : Gradle

Incompatible change type : source

Short summary : Kotlin 2.4.0 removes deprecated Gradle APIs related to selecting the legacy Kotlin/JS compiler type.

Additionally, the KotlinJsCompilerType enum and the KotlinProjectExtension.js() overloads with a compiler type parameter are deprecated. To migrate, remove the compiler type argument from the js() target declaration and use the js {} block instead.

Deprecation cycle :

1.8.0: deprecate legacy Kotlin/JS compiler type constants

2.4.0: remove the deprecated legacy compiler type APIs and report a warning when using KotlinJsCompilerType or KotlinProjectExtension.js() overloads with a compiler type parameter

candidates.text:
Use JavaScript code from Kotlin

Kotlin was first designed for easy interoperation with the Java platform: it sees Java classes as Kotlin classes, and Java sees Kotlin classes as Java classes.

However, JavaScript is a dynamically typed language, which means it does not check types at compile time. You can freely talk to JavaScript from Kotlin via dynamic types. If you want to use the full power of the Kotlin type system, you can create external declarations for JavaScript libraries which will be understood by the Kotlin compiler and the surrounding tooling.
candidates.title: Use JavaScript code from Kotlin
sections: Use JavaScript code from Kotlin

candidates.text:
Isolating declarations in a separate JavaScript object in plain mode

If you have explicitly set your module kind to be plain , Kotlin creates an object that contains all Kotlin declarations from the current module. This is done to prevent spoiling the global object. This means that for a module myModule , all declarations are available to JavaScript via the myModule object. For example:

fun foo() = "Hello"

This function can be called from JavaScript like this:

alert(myModule.foo());

Calling the function directly like this is not applicable when you compile your Kotlin module to JavaScript modules like UMD (the default setting for both browser and nodejs targets), ESM , CommonJS , or AMD . In these cases, your declarations are exposed according to the chosen JavaScript module system. For example, when using UMD, ESM, or CommonJS, your call site would look like this:

alert(require('myModule').foo());
candidates.title: Use Kotlin code from JavaScript
sections: Use Kotlin code from JavaScript > Isolating declarations in a separate JavaScript object in plain mode

candidates.text:
Package structure

For most of the module systems (CommonJS, Plain, and UMD), Kotlin exposes its package structure to JavaScript. Unless you define your declarations in the root package, you have to use fully qualified names in JavaScript. For example:

package my.qualified.packagename

fun foo() = "Hello"

For example, when using UMD or CommonJS, your call site could look like this:

alert(require('myModule').my.qualified.packagename.foo())

When using plain as a module system setting, the call site would be:

alert(myModule.my.qualified.packagename.foo());

When targeting ECMAScript Modules (ESM), package information is not preserved to improve the application bundle size and match the typical layout of ESM packages. In this case, the consumption of the Kotlin declarations with ES modules looks like this:

import { foo } from 'myModule';

alert(foo());

candidates.text:
Declare parameters with default values

If you are writing an external declaration for a JavaScript function which has a parameter with a default value, use definedExternally . This delegates the generation of the default values to the JavaScript function itself:

external fun myFunWithOptionalArgs(
    x: Int,
    y: String = definedExternally,
    z: String = definedExternally
)

With this external declaration, you can call myFunWithOptionalArgs with one required argument and two optional arguments, where the default values are calculated by the JavaScript implementation of myFunWithOptionalArgs .

result.answer: Use the `external` modifier to declare an existing JavaScript API so Kotlin can call it [1]. For APIs whose parameters are expected to support certain methods, express that concept with an `external interface` [1]. A typical use case for external interfaces is to describe settings objects, as illustrated by `JQueryAjaxSettings` [1]. You can also declare an `external class` with a `companion object` function, as in `external class JQuery { companion object { fun get(settings: JQueryAjaxSettings): JQueryXHR } }`, and then call it from Kotlin [1]. Note that JavaScript does not have the concept of interfaces; when a function expects its parameter to support two methods `foo` and `bar`, you would just pass in an object that actually has these methods [1].

quotes.text:
external interfaces

JavaScript does not have the concept of interfaces. When a function expects its parameter to support two methods foo and bar , you would just pass in an object that actually has these methods.

You can use interfaces to express this concept in statically typed Kotlin:

external interface HasFooAndBar {
    fun foo()

    fun bar()
}

external fun myFunction(p: HasFooAndBar)

Use the `@JsName` annotation to control the generated JavaScript name for an exported declaration [2]. The Kotlin compiler otherwise mangles the names of generated functions and attributes in JavaScript code — for example, without `@JsName` the corresponding function name would contain a suffix calculated from the function signature, such as `hello_61zpoe$` [2][4]. `@JsName` likewise lets you specify the names for the generated and exported functions, which helps resolve ambiguities in exports like overloads for functions with the same name [1].

The parameter of `@JsName` is required to be a constant string literal which is a valid identifier; the compiler reports an error for a non-identifier string [4].

Kotlin-only example:
```kotlin
class Person(val name: String) {
    fun hello() {
        println("Hello $name!")
    }

    @JsName("helloWithGreeting")
    fun hello(greeting: String) {
        println("$greeting $name!")
    }
}
```
This example is taken verbatim from the documentation, where the client uses `person.hello()` and `person.helloWithGreeting("Servus")` [2].

If your goal is a default export specifically, a separate annotation `@JsExport.Default` applied to a Kotlin declaration (class, object, function, or property) makes the generated JavaScript automatically include an `export default` statement for ES modules; for module systems different from ES modules, `@JsExport.Default` works similarly to the regular `@JsExport` annotation [3].

Yes, but only in the supported suspending-lambda scenario shown here, and the feature requires enabling a compiler option. }

Can I export a class for the client in the same way?

Answer
Yes. Applying the `@JsExport` annotation to a top-level declaration (like a class, interface, or function) makes Kotlin declarations available from JavaScript or TypeScript, and the annotation exports all nested declarations with the name given in Kotlin [1]. How should I give an exported declaration a predictable JavaScript name?

Answer
Use the `@JsName` annotation to control the generated JavaScript name for an exported declaration [2]. The Kotlin compiler otherwise mangles the names of generated functions and attributes in JavaScript code — for example, without `@JsName` the corresponding function name would contain a suffix calculated from the function signature, such as `hello_61zpoe$` [2][4]. `@JsName` likewise lets you specify the names for the generated and exported functions, which helps resolve ambiguities in exports like overloads for functions with the same name [1].

The parameter of `@JsName` is required to be a constant string literal which is a valid identifier; the compiler reports an error for a non-identifier string [4].

Kotlin-only example:
```kotlin
class Person(val name: String) {
    fun hello() {
        println("Hello $name!")
    }

    @JsName("helloWithGreeting")
    fun hello(greeting: String) {
        println("$greeting $name!")
    }
}
```
This example is taken verbatim from the documentation, where the client uses `person.hello()` and `person.helloWithGreeting("Servus")` [2].

If your goal is a default export specifically, a separate annotation `@JsExport.Default` applied to a Kotlin declaration (class, object, function, or property) makes the generated JavaScript automatically include an `export default` statement for ES modules; for module systems different from ES modules, `@JsExport.Default` works similarly to the regular `@JsExport` annotation [3].

Yes, but only in the supported suspending-lambda scenario shown here, and the feature requires enabling a compiler option. To export Kotlin's suspending lambda expressions as JavaScript async functions, add the compiler option `-Xsuspend-lambda-exporting` to your build.gradle.kts [1], and mark the relevant Kotlin declarations with the `@JsExport` annotation [1]. After that, the suspend lambda is mapped to a regular async function on the TypeScript/JavaScript side, so the client can pass an async lambda and await the result [3][2].

Kotlin-only example (as shown in the documentation):

```kotlin
@JsExport
class TaskRunner {
    suspend fun runTask(task: suspend () -> String): String {
        return task()
    }
}
```

This example is taken verbatim from the documentation [1][2].

Important limitation from the evidence: with Kotlin 2.4.20, you can export suspending lambda expressions as JavaScript async functions, and previously there was no way to export declarations containing suspending lambdas from Kotlin/JS libraries [4]. The retrieved sources describe only this suspending-lambda export path; they do not state whether non-suspending lambdas can be passed from the client.

external interfaces

JavaScript does not have the concept of interfaces. When a function expects its parameter to support two methods foo and bar , you would just pass in an object that actually has these methods.

You can use interfaces to express this concept in statically typed Kotlin:

external interface HasFooAndBar {
    fun foo()

    fun bar()
}

external fun myFunction(p: HasFooAndBar)

A typical use case for external interfaces is to describe settings objects. For example:

external interface JQueryAjaxSettings {
    var async: Boolean

    var cache: Boolean

    var complete: (JQueryXHR, String) -> Unit

    // etc
}

fun JQueryAjaxSettings(): JQueryAjaxSettings = js("{}")

external class JQuery {
    companion object {
        fun get(settings: JQueryAjaxSettings): JQueryXHR
    }
}

fun sendQuery() {
    JQuery.get(JQueryAjaxSettings().apply {
        complete = { (xhr, data) ->
            window.alert("Request complete")
        }
    })
}

sections: Use JavaScript code from Kotlin > external modifier > external interfaces

candidates.text:
external modifier

To tell Kotlin that a certain declaration is written in pure JavaScript, you should mark it with the external modifier. When the compiler sees such a declaration, it assumes that the implementation for the corresponding class, function or property is provided externally (by the developer or via an npm dependency ), and therefore does not try to generate any JavaScript code from the declaration. This is also why external declarations can't have a body. For example:

external fun alert(message: Any?): Unit

external class Node {
    val firstChild: Node

    fun append(child: Node): Node

    fun removeChild(child: Node): Node

    // etc
}

external val window: Window

Note that the external modifier is inherited by nested declarations. This is why in the example Node class, there is no external modifier before member functions and properties.

The external modifier is only allowed on package-level declarations. You can't declare an external member of a non- external class.

candidates.text:
External interfaces have some restrictions:

They can't be used on the right-hand side of is checks.

They can't be passed as reified type arguments.

They can't be used in class literal expressions (such as I::class ).

as casts to external interfaces always succeed. Casting to external interfaces produces the "Unchecked cast to external interface" compile time warning. The warning can be suppressed with the @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST_TO_EXTERNAL_INTERFACE") annotation.

IntelliJ IDEA can also automatically generate the @Suppress annotation. Open the intentions menu via the light bulb icon or Alt-Enter, and click the small arrow next to the "Unchecked cast to external interface" inspection. Here, you can select the suppression scope, and your IDE will add the annotation to your file accordingly.

candidates.text:
Declare parameters with default values

If you are writing an external declaration for a JavaScript function which has a parameter with a default value, use definedExternally . This delegates the generation of the default values to the JavaScript function itself:

external fun myFunWithOptionalArgs(
    x: Int,
    y: String = definedExternally,
    z: String = definedExternally
)

With this external declaration, you can call myFunWithOptionalArgs with one required argument and two optional arguments, where the default values are calculated by the JavaScript implementation of myFunWithOptionalArgs .

candidates.text:
Isolating declarations in a separate JavaScript object in plain mode

If you have explicitly set your module kind to be plain , Kotlin creates an object that contains all Kotlin declarations from the current module. This is done to prevent spoiling the global object. This means that for a module myModule , all declarations are available to JavaScript via the myModule object. For example:

fun foo() = "Hello"

This function can be called from JavaScript like this:

alert(myModule.foo());

Calling the function directly like this is not applicable when you compile your Kotlin module to JavaScript modules like UMD (the default setting for both browser and nodejs targets), ESM , CommonJS , or AMD . In these cases, your declarations are exposed according to the chosen JavaScript module system. For example, when using UMD, ESM, or CommonJS, your call site would look like this:

alert(require('myModule').foo());

candidates.text:
Use JavaScript code from Kotlin

Kotlin was first designed for easy interoperation with the Java platform: it sees Java classes as Kotlin classes, and Java sees Kotlin classes as Java classes.

However, JavaScript is a dynamically typed language, which means it does not check types at compile time. You can freely talk to JavaScript from Kotlin via dynamic types. If you want to use the full power of the Kotlin type system, you can create external declarations for JavaScript libraries which will be understood by the Kotlin compiler and the surrounding tooling.

If we didn't specify the @JsName annotation, the name of the corresponding function would contain a suffix calculated from the function signature, for example hello_61zpoe$ .

Note that there are some cases in which the Kotlin compiler does not apply mangling:

external declarations are not mangled.

Any overridden functions in non- external classes inheriting from external classes are not mangled.

The parameter of @JsName is required to be a constant string literal which is a valid identifier. The compiler will report an error on any attempt to pass a non-identifier string to @JsName . The following example produces a compile-time error:

candidates.text:
Package structure

For most of the module systems (CommonJS, Plain, and UMD), Kotlin exposes its package structure to JavaScript. Unless you define your declarations in the root package, you have to use fully qualified names in JavaScript. For example:

package my.qualified.packagename

fun foo() = "Hello"

For example, when using UMD or CommonJS, your call site could look like this:

alert(require('myModule').my.qualified.packagename.foo())

When using plain as a module system setting, the call site would be:

alert(myModule.my.qualified.packagename.foo());

When targeting ECMAScript Modules (ESM), package information is not preserved to improve the application bundle size and match the typical layout of ESM packages. In this case, the consumption of the Kotlin declarations with ES modules looks like this:

import { foo } from 'myModule';

alert(foo());

chunks.text:
Use JavaScript code from Kotlin

Kotlin was first designed for easy interoperation with the Java platform: it sees Java classes as Kotlin classes, and Java sees Kotlin classes as Java classes.

However, JavaScript is a dynamically typed language, which means it does not check types at compile time. You can freely talk to JavaScript from Kotlin via dynamic types. If you want to use the full power of the Kotlin type system, you can create external declarations for JavaScript libraries which will be understood by the Kotlin compiler and the surrounding tooling.

result.answer: JavaScript has no concept of interfaces; when a function expects its parameter to support two methods foo and bar, you would just pass in an object that actually has these methods [1]. You express that concept in statically typed Kotlin with interfaces, e.g. an external interface declaring `fun foo()` and `fun bar()` and then `external fun myFunction(p: HasFooAndBar)` [1]. A typical use case for external interfaces is to describe settings objects, such as `external interface JQueryAjaxSettings` with properties `var async: Boolean`, `var cache: Boolean`, and `var complete: (JQueryXHR, String) -> Unit` [1]. Such a settings object can be constructed on the Kotlin side with `fun JQueryAjaxSettings(): JQueryAjaxSettings = js("{}")` and used via an `external class JQuery { companion object { fun get(settings: JQueryAjaxSettings): JQueryXHR } }`, then called in `fun sendQuery() { JQuery.get(JQueryAjaxSettings().apply { complete = { (xhr, data) -> window.alert("Request complete") } }) }` [1]. External interfaces also have restrictions: they can't be used on the right-hand side of `is` checks [2], they can't be passed as reified type arguments [2], they can't be used in class literal expressions (such as `I::class`) [2], and `as` casts to external interfaces always succeed, producing the "Unchecked cast to external interface" compile time warning which can be suppressed with `@Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST_TO_EXTERNAL_INTERFACE")` [2].

Use the `@JsName` annotation to control the generated JavaScript name for an exported declaration [2]. The Kotlin compiler otherwise mangles the names of generated functions and attributes in JavaScript code — for example, without `@JsName` the corresponding function name would contain a suffix calculated from the function signature, such as `hello_61zpoe$` [2][4]. `@JsName` likewise lets you specify the names for the generated and exported functions, which helps resolve ambiguities in exports like overloads for functions with the same name [1].

The parameter of `@JsName` is required to be a constant string literal which is a valid identifier; the compiler reports an error for a non-identifier string [4].

Kotlin-only example:
```kotlin
class Person(val name: String) {
    fun hello() {
        println("Hello $name!")
    }

    @JsName("helloWithGreeting")
    fun hello(greeting: String) {
        println("$greeting $name!")
    }
}
```
This example is taken verbatim from the documentation, where the client uses `person.hello()` and `person.helloWithGreeting("Servus")` [2].

If your goal is a default export specifically, a separate annotation `@JsExport.Default` applied to a Kotlin declaration (class, object, function, or property) makes the generated JavaScript automatically include an `export default` statement for ES modules; for module systems different from ES modules, `@JsExport.Default` works similarly to the regular `@JsExport` annotation [3].

Yes, but only in the supported suspending-lambda scenario shown here, and the feature requires enabling a compiler option. To export Kotlin's suspending lambda expressions as JavaScript async functions, add the compiler option `-Xsuspend-lambda-exporting` to your build.gradle.kts [1], and mark the relevant Kotlin declarations with the `@JsExport` annotation [1]. After that, the suspend lambda is mapped to a regular async function on the TypeScript/JavaScript side, so the client can pass an async lambda and await the result [3][2].

Kotlin-only example (as shown in the documentation):

```kotlin
@JsExport
class TaskRunner {
    suspend fun runTask(task: suspend () -> String): String {
        return task()
    }
}
```

This example is taken verbatim from the documentation [1][2].

Important limitation from the evidence: with Kotlin 2.4.20, you can export suspending lambda expressions as JavaScript async functions, and previously there was no way to export declarations containing suspending lambdas from Kotlin/JS libraries [4]. For APIs whose parameters are expected to support certain methods, express that concept with an `external interface` [1]. Can I export a class for the client in the same way?

Answer
Yes. Applying the `@JsExport` annotation to a top-level declaration (like a class, interface, or function) makes Kotlin declarations available from JavaScript or TypeScript, and the annotation exports all nested declarations with the name given in Kotlin [1]. Regular Kotlin classes can be exported to JavaScript/TypeScript [3], and you can export a value class as a regular TypeScript class by marking it with `@JsExport` (together with `@JvmInline`) [2].

How should I give an exported declaration a predictable JavaScript name?

Answer
Use the `@JsName` annotation to control the generated JavaScript name for an exported declaration [2]. The Kotlin compiler otherwise mangles the names of generated functions and attributes in JavaScript code — for example, without `@JsName` the corresponding function name would contain a suffix calculated from the function signature, such as `hello_61zpoe$` [2][4]. `@JsName` likewise lets you specify the names for the generated and exported functions, which helps resolve ambiguities in exports like overloads for functions with the same name [1].

The parameter of `@JsName` is required to be a constant string literal which is a valid identifier; the compiler reports an error for a non-identifier string [4].

Kotlin-only example:
```kotlin
class Person(val name: String) {
    fun hello() {
        println("Hello $name!")
    }

    @JsName("helloWithGreeting")
    fun hello(greeting: String) {
        println("$greeting $name!")
    }
}
```
This example is taken verbatim from the documentation, where the client uses `person.hello()` and `person.helloWithGreeting("Servus")` [2].

If your goal is a default export specifically, a separate annotation `@JsExport.Default` applied to a Kotlin declaration (class, object, function, or property) makes the generated JavaScript automatically include an `export default` statement for ES modules; for module systems different from ES modules, `@JsExport.Default` works similarly to the regular `@JsExport` annotation [3].

How do I declare an existing JavaScript API so Kotlin can call it?

Answer
Use the `external` modifier to declare an existing JavaScript API so Kotlin can call it [1]. For APIs whose parameters are expected to support certain methods, express that concept with an `external interface` [1]. A typical use case for external interfaces is to describe settings objects, as illustrated by `JQueryAjaxSettings` [1]. You can also declare an `external class` with a `companion object` function, as in `external class JQuery { companion object { fun get(settings: JQueryAjaxSettings): JQueryXHR } }`, and then call it from Kotlin [1]. Note that JavaScript does not have the concept of interfaces; when a function expects its parameter to support two methods `foo` and `bar`, you would just pass in an object that actually has these methods [1].

Yes, but only in the supported suspending-lambda scenario shown here, and the feature requires enabling a compiler option. To export Kotlin's suspending lambda expressions as JavaScript async functions, add the compiler option `-Xsuspend-lambda-exporting` to your build.gradle.kts [1], and mark the relevant Kotlin declarations with the `@JsExport` annotation [1]. After that, the suspend lambda is mapped to a regular async function on the TypeScript/JavaScript side, so the client can pass an async lambda and await the result [3][2].

Kotlin-only example (as shown in the documentation):

```kotlin
@JsExport
class TaskRunner {
    suspend fun runTask(task: suspend () -> String): String {
        return task()
    }
}
```

This example is taken verbatim from the documentation [1][2].

Important limitation from the evidence: with Kotlin 2.4.20, you can export suspending lambda expressions as JavaScript async functions, and previously there was no way to export declarations containing suspending lambdas from Kotlin/JS libraries [4]. Use the `external` modifier to declare an existing JavaScript API so Kotlin can call it [1]. external interfaces

JavaScript does not have the concept of interfaces. When a function expects its parameter to support two methods foo and bar , you would just pass in an object that actually has these methods.

You can use interfaces to express this concept in statically typed Kotlin:

external interface HasFooAndBar {
    fun foo()

    fun bar()
}

external fun myFunction(p: HasFooAndBar)

A typical use case for external interfaces is to describe settings objects. For example:

external interface JQueryAjaxSettings {
    var async: Boolean

    var cache: Boolean

    var complete: (JQueryXHR, String) -> Unit

    // etc
}

fun JQueryAjaxSettings(): JQueryAjaxSettings = js("{}")

external class JQuery {
    companion object {
        fun get(settings: JQueryAjaxSettings): JQueryXHR
    }
}

fun sendQuery() {
    JQuery.get(JQueryAjaxSettings().apply {
        complete = { (xhr, data) ->
            window.alert("Request complete")
        }
    })
}

candidates.text:
external modifier

To tell Kotlin that a certain declaration is written in pure JavaScript, you should mark it with the external modifier. When the compiler sees such a declaration, it assumes that the implementation for the corresponding class, function or property is provided externally (by the developer or via an npm dependency ), and therefore does not try to generate any JavaScript code from the declaration. This is also why external declarations can't have a body. For example:

external fun alert(message: Any?): Unit

external class Node {
    val firstChild: Node

    fun append(child: Node): Node

    fun removeChild(child: Node): Node

    // etc
}

external val window: Window

Note that the external modifier is inherited by nested declarations. This is why in the example Node class, there is no external modifier before member functions and properties.

The external modifier is only allowed on package-level declarations. You can't declare an external member of a non- external class.

candidates.text:
Declare parameters with default values

If you are writing an external declaration for a JavaScript function which has a parameter with a default value, use definedExternally . This delegates the generation of the default values to the JavaScript function itself:

external fun myFunWithOptionalArgs(
    x: Int,
    y: String = definedExternally,
    z: String = definedExternally
)

With this external declaration, you can call myFunWithOptionalArgs with one required argument and two optional arguments, where the default values are calculated by the JavaScript implementation of myFunWithOptionalArgs .

If we didn't specify the @JsName annotation, the name of the corresponding function would contain a suffix calculated from the function signature, for example hello_61zpoe$ .

Note that there are some cases in which the Kotlin compiler does not apply mangling:

external declarations are not mangled.

Any overridden functions in non- external classes inheriting from external classes are not mangled.

The parameter of @JsName is required to be a constant string literal which is a valid identifier. The compiler will report an error on any attempt to pass a non-identifier string to @JsName . The following example produces a compile-time error:

@JsName("new C()")   // error here

candidates.text:
Isolating declarations in a separate JavaScript object in plain mode

If you have explicitly set your module kind to be plain , Kotlin creates an object that contains all Kotlin declarations from the current module. This is done to prevent spoiling the global object. This means that for a module myModule , all declarations are available to JavaScript via the myModule object. For example:

fun foo() = "Hello"

This function can be called from JavaScript like this:

alert(myModule.foo());

Calling the function directly like this is not applicable when you compile your Kotlin module to JavaScript modules like UMD (the default setting for both browser and nodejs targets), ESM , CommonJS , or AMD . In these cases, your declarations are exposed according to the chosen JavaScript module system. For example, when using UMD, ESM, or CommonJS, your call site would look like this:

alert(require('myModule').foo());

Kotlin types in JavaScript

See how Kotlin types are mapped to JavaScript ones:

Kotlin | JavaScript | Comments
Byte , Short , Int , Float , Double | Number | 
Char | Number | The number represents the character's code.
Long | BigInt | Set target = "es2020" or configure the -Xes-long-as-bigint compiler option .
Boolean | Boolean | 
String | String | 
Array | Array | 
ByteArray | Int8Array | 
ShortArray | Int16Array | 
IntArray | Int32Array | 
CharArray | UInt16Array | Carries the property $type$ == "CharArray" .
FloatArray | Float32Array | 
DoubleArray | Float64Array | 
LongArray | BigInt64Array | Set target = "es2020" or configure the -Xes-long-as-bigint compiler option .
BooleanArray | Int8Array | Carries the property $type$ == "BooleanArray" .
List , MutableList | KtList , KtMutableList | Exposes an Array via KtList.asJsReadonlyArrayView or KtMutableList.asJsArrayView .
Map , MutableMap | KtMap , KtMutableMap | Exposes an ES2015 Map via KtMap.asJsReadonlyMapView or KtMutableMap.asJsMapView .
Set , MutableSet | KtSet , KtMutableSet | Exposes an ES2015 Set via KtSet.asJsReadonlySetView or KtMutableSet.asJsSetView .
Unit | undefined | Exportable when used as return type, but not when used as parameter type.
Any | Object | 
Throwable | Error | 
enum class Type | Type | Enum entries are exposed as static class properties ( Type.ENTRY ).
Nullable Type? | Type , null , or undefined | 
All other Kotlin types, except for those marked with @JsExport | Not supported | Includes Kotlin's unsigned integer types .
